changes.before: If the text changes to "90" without a unit, what happens?
changes.after: Read a length of time from text with units.

before: time.Duration represents a signed nanosecond count. time.ParseDuration accepts unit-marked text such as 1m30s and returns a duration plus an error. A bare number without a unit is not interpreted as minutes.

This example converts a fixed duration to seconds using Seconds, which returns float64. It does not call time.Now or sleep. For calendar events, location and date rules are separate concerns; duration arithmetic alone does not model daylight-saving transitions.
Expected output or behavior: 90. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Try a fractional second and explain its representation without measuring elapsed wall-clock time. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A duration is an amount of time. Go stores it as a count of nanoseconds; one nanosecond is one billionth of a second. `time.ParseDuration` reads text such as `1m30s` and returns a duration or an error.
`Seconds()` gives the duration as a float64 number of seconds. The program converts a fixed amount of time; it does not wait or check a clock.
The screen shows `90`. One minute and thirty seconds is ninety seconds.
A nonzero number needs a unit, such as s for seconds. Durations describe amounts of time; calendar dates and time zones follow separate rules.
